title: Blackdamp
subtitle: Ottway, Selden County, West Virginia, April 1927

listing.title: Blackdamp ⛏️
listing.blurb: West Virginia, April 1927. Ottway is a coal camp at the head of a hollow, and the company owns all of it: the houses, the store, the scrip in your pocket and the men with badges at the drift mouth. Eight years ago a section of the mine called 7 North blew up, and the company sealed it with men still inside. Now the miners are meeting in secret, the guards are walking the tipple at night, and something is coming up out of the sealed workings to take anyone it finds alone in the dark. On Monday morning the fire boss hears knocking behind the seal: a man, alive. The company says it is the mountain settling. Levels 3–6.

synopsis: Ottway is a company town of nine hundred people in the smokeless coalfield of southern West Virginia, strung for a mile and a half along Kettle Run below Shumate Ridge, at the end of a railroad branch fourteen miles from the county seat at Gale. The Ottway Smokeless Coal Company, owned by the Ottway family of Philadelphia, owns everything in it: the mine, the tipple and the coke ovens, three hundred board-and-batten houses in five rows, the store, the doctor, the church lots, the road and the right to say who walks on it. Miners are paid by the ton in company scrip, good only at the company store, and most of them owe the store more than they earn. Ottway No. 3 is a drift mine driven into the ridge. On Tuesday 14 October 1919 a gas explosion and fire at the face of a section called 7 North cut off fourteen men. The company's list of the dead had thirteen names: the fourteenth, Ezell Pettaway, a young Black loader, worked on another man's check and so did not exist on the company's books. The next day the mine foreman, Elwood Bledsoe, had 7 North sealed with masonry stoppings to smother the fire, which is accepted practice. What the inquest did not hear is that the men were not dead. They had barricaded themselves at the foot of the old Number Two air shaft, where air seeped down through a rotten timber cap and a grey thread of daylight came through it at noon, and for nine days they knocked on the track rail the old signal for men alive. The seal crew heard them. Bledsoe told them it was squeeze, the mountain settling. On the third day, on a telegram from Philadelphia, company men poured two feet of concrete over the air shaft to starve the fire of air. The knocking went on six more days, fainter, and on 23 October 1919 it stopped. When the light went out of their room, something came into the dark with them. The last of them, Lafe Combs, died alone in it, and it did not stop. The lamp man, Imre Halász, never took the fourteen brass checks off the board, and from the day of the seal he kept a flame safety lamp burning under them, every shift, for seven and a half years, because the men had not been counted up. On 1 March 1927, with organizers from the United Mine Workers in the hollow and the company bringing in the Ironwood Detective Agency's guards to break them, the new guard captain cleared the old check board and put the Kept Light out. Three weeks later a guard walking the tipple alone vanished, and two union men were jailed for his murder. The party arrive on Friday 8 April. On Sunday night a young miner walking home alone from the union's secret meeting is taken, and at ten past three on Monday morning the fire boss hears knocking behind the 7 North seal. A man is alive back there, and he has nine days, the nine days the fourteen had. The company will not open the seal. The miners want it opened. And every night the thing that began behind it comes a little further up the hollow. Blackdamp is a horror campaign about a company town at the edge of a strike, a crime eight years old, and the one rule the dark has to follow: it can only take you if you are alone.
hook: The mixed train up the Kettle Run branch, Friday 8 April 1927, four in the afternoon. It is two coaches and a string of empty coal hoppers behind a tired engine, and it climbs for an hour through a hollow so narrow that the dogwood on one bank nearly touches the redbud on the other, past six coal camps that all look the same: the tipple, the coke ovens smoking in a long row of glowing mouths, the store, the rows of grey houses up the hillsides, washing on the lines going grey too. Everyone left on the train at the end of the line is going to Ottway. A Pittsburgh reporter with a letter that has no signature. The new company doctor with an inquest transcript he took from his father's shelf. A cutting-machine man back from six years in the steel mills, who has come to bring his brother home. A mine guard with a badge pinned crooked, coming back from Gale. A granny midwife who rode down to Gale to deliver a baby and is riding back up. A ridge farmer with a rifle and a sack of seed potatoes, who has seen a light walking in her upper pasture where nothing should be walking. At the Ottway depot two Ironwood men with shotguns check everyone who gets off, and a man in a good suit from the company office takes the doctor's bag for him and looks at the reporter's camera for a long, careful moment. Up the hollow the coke ovens glow under the drift mouth, and in the lamp house beside it, under a new board of electric cap lamps all charging in their racks, there is a darker rectangle on the wall where an older board hung for twenty years. Tomorrow is payday.

setting.name: Ottway and Shumate Ridge, Selden County, West Virginia, 8 April to 1 May 1927
setting.description: Ottway, Kettle Run, Shumate Ridge, Selden County, the town of Gale, the Ottway Smokeless Coal Company, the Ironwood Detective Agency, Local 5512 and everyone in the campaign are fictional; the coalfields, the year and the history are real. In 1927 the smokeless and high-volatile coalfields of southern West Virginia are almost entirely non-union. The mine wars of 1912 to 1921, the tent colonies, the armed marches and the treason trials that followed, are fresh memory in every camp, and every man over twenty-five has a story. The coal operators run their camps with private guards from detective agencies, deputised by county sheriffs whose offices the operators pay for; miners sign 'yellow-dog' contracts swearing never to join a union; men are paid by the ton, in scrip, often weighed by the company's own weighman, and charged by the company for rent, powder, carbide, blacksmithing, the doctor and the store. In April 1927 the union's contracts in the northern fields have expired and a long strike has begun there; organizers are slipping into the southern camps at night, and the companies are evicting any family they catch. The workforce is native West Virginians and Kentuckians from the hill farms, Black miners recruited from Alabama, Virginia and the Carolinas, and Italian, Hungarian, Polish and Slovak immigrants. They live in separate rows, go to separate churches and send their children to separate schools, by company and county design, and they go down the same drift mouth every morning and depend on each other for their lives.
setting.atmosphere: Coal smoke, coke-oven glow, rain and mud. The hollow is so narrow and steep that the sun reaches the bottom only between ten and three, and the camp lives in a grey half-light under a lid of smoke; at night the long row of coke ovens burns orange along the creek like a street of open doors, and everything beyond their light is black. Sounds: the tipple's shaker screens, coal cars banging, the motor's whine in the drift mouth, the shift whistle at six, a dog at every house, a Hungarian hymn and a gospel hymn from two churches a quarter mile apart on a Sunday night, the creek always running. April smells of rain, sulphur, wild leeks cooking in iron pans, wet wool, carbide and dogwood. People are warm, proud, wary, funny, tired, in debt, and watching who talks to whom. Horror here is quiet and close: a lamp flame going blue and small, a voice you know calling your name from a dark stretch of path, knocking under a kitchen floor, the moment you realise you can no longer hear the person who was walking beside you.

regions.name: The Bottom and the Drift Mouth
regions.description: The working heart of the camp at the head of the hollow: the drift mouth of Ottway No. 3 cut into the foot of Shumate Ridge, with the haulage track running out of it to the tipple; the tipple itself, a tall black timber tower of screens and chutes over the railroad siding; the lamp house beside the drift mouth, where every man takes his lamp and hangs his brass check, now with a new rack of Edison electric cap lamps; the guards' shanty; the powder magazine, a stone hut half dug into the bank; the long battery of beehive coke ovens along the creek, a hundred and twenty brick domes glowing day and night; the slate dump, a grey hill of waste rock that smokes in wet weather; and the company office, a brick building with bars on the pay window, where Superintendent Elwood Bledsoe has his desk.

regions.name: The Rows
regions.description: Five rows of company houses up the slopes on both sides of Kettle Run, all painted the same company grey, each a four-room box on posts with a coal house and a privy behind it and a garden plot where people grow beans and potatoes in every inch. Number One and Number Two Bottom, by the creek, are the native and immigrant miners' rows, and Lettie Burchett's house is the last on Number Two, nearest the drift mouth. Across the creek and up the hill is the Black miners' row the company calls Number Four and everyone calls the Hill, with Mount Moriah Baptist Church and the Colored School at its head; further down, the Hungarian and Slovak families' St. Stephen's, a white frame church with an onion-shaped tin cupola. Highest of all, on the dry side of the hollow with the only paved walk and the only street lamps in Ottway, is the boss row, five painted houses with porches, which the camp calls Silk Stocking Row.

regions.name: The Company Store and the Depot
regions.description: Down the hollow, at the end of the branch line: the Ottway depot and its water tank; the company store, a long two-storey brick building with a porch, the post office window, a soda fountain, a pharmacy counter, a meat cooler, furniture, coffins and dress goods, and upstairs the scrip office and the ledger room, run by store manager Vinton Plumley; the doctor's office and four-bed infirmary behind it; the company's electric plant, which lights the boss row, the office, the store and the drift mouth and nothing else; the boarding house for single men; the baseball field. A road, the only road, climbs out of the hollow to the county road and Gale, fourteen miles; Ironwood men sit in a car at the top of it, at the place the camp calls the dead line.

regions.name: Shumate Ridge and Gale
regions.description: Above the camp the ridge rises seven hundred feet through second-growth oak, poplar and laurel to the Shumate farm on top: forty acres of steep pasture, an apple orchard, a log house with a frame addition, a spring house, and, in the upper pasture inside a fallen fence, the concrete cap of the old Number Two air shaft, fourteen feet square and stamped with a date. On the far side of the farm, in a laurel thicket, is the mouth of the Shumates' own country coal bank, dug in the 1880s for house coal. Under the ridge lies the whole of Ottway No. 3, and 7 North under its northern shoulder. Fourteen miles down the valley is Gale, the county seat: a courthouse with a jail behind it, two banks, a newspaper (the Selden County Banner), the railroad junction, a Western Union office, a telephone exchange, a hotel and a lawyer on every corner, most of them on retainer to a coal company.

campaignRules.name: The Nine-Day Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs from Friday 8 April to Sunday 1 May 1927, and two clocks run at once. THE NINE DAYS: whoever the Dark takes is held alive in the room where it began for nine days and nine nights, the nine days the fourteen lasted in 1919 (Rule 4, below), and then is gone. Lester Gaither, the Ironwood guard taken on Friday 25 March, was alive behind the seal until the night of Sunday 3 April, and his knocking was heard by the fire boss from 28 March to 3 April and then stopped; he is beyond help when the campaign begins. Dewey Spradlin, taken on Sunday 10 April at about eleven at night on the creek path, can be brought out alive until midnight on Tuesday 19 April. Anyone else the Dark takes during play gets nine days from the hour they were taken. Tell the players the date every morning; let them count. THE COMPANY'S CALENDAR: Sat 9 Apr payday (settlement day, and the bobtail checks). Sun 10 Apr: Local 5512 meets at Mount Moriah after the evening service. Mon 11 Apr, 3:10 a.m.: the knocking at the 7 North seal. Tue 12 Apr: the first three evictions. Thu 14 Apr: the Local's vote on whether to come out on strike unless 7 North is opened. Sat 16 Apr: the Gale grand jury meets on the Gaither murder charge. Mon 18 Apr: the company's notice that every man must sign the new contract or vacate. Sat 30 Apr: moving day, when every house of a man who has not signed is to be emptied onto the road. Mon 2 May: the company reopens 7 North, with a crew of new men from outside and Ironwood guards. CLEAR NOON: the hollow is overcast or raining at midday on every day of the campaign except Saturday 9 April, Friday 22 April, Thursday 28 April and Sunday 1 May, which matters for Rule 6. If the party never act, the company's crew goes into 7 North on 2 May, men are alone in the dark at the face within the hour, and Ottway No. 3 loses its second section.

campaignRules.name: The Blackdamp's Rules (GM only)
campaignRules.description: The thing from 7 North is The Hungry Dark (adversaries.json; LookupMonster) and the old miners, when they say anything, call it the blackdamp, the miners' word for the dead air that puts your lamp out before it kills you. It follows rules, and the GM never changes them once the players have learned one; each has three or more clues (controlFile.clues). RULE 1, WHAT CALLED IT: a light that had always been kept burning for the dead, put out. From 15 October 1919 the lamp man Imre Halász kept a flame safety lamp lit under the fourteen brass checks on the lamp-house board; on 1 March 1927 Captain Kincaid's men pinched it out and threw the checks on the slate dump. It began in the barricade room on Friday 17 October 1919, when the cap was poured and the last grey daylight went out of that room; in the six days after, it took the fourteen who went anywhere alone, and last of all Lafe Combs, alone, on 23 October. The Kept Light, already burning, held it below ground for seven and a half years, and the night it went out, it started up. RULE 2, ONLY THE ALONE: it can take only a person who is alone in the dark, with no other living person within arm's reach or answering voice (30 feet, and able to hear each other) and no light of their own. Two people together are never taken, even in pitch dark, and a rope tied between them counts as together at any length while they can hear each other. It will work to separate people: Drink the Light, a stone falling, and the voice of the last person it took calling for help from the dark (Dewey's voice, from 10 April). RULE 3, LIGHT: it moves only through unbroken darkness and cannot enter bright light; bright light and fire burn it (fire and daylight do double damage; it resists ordinary weapons). A single flame is dim and it can put that out; an electric lamp is bright for 10 feet, a bonfire for 30, and the coke ovens' row and the lit boss row are walls it cannot cross. Each night, it rises from 7 North through the old workings and the drift mouth and goes where the dark is continuous. Reduced to 0 hit points it breaks into ordinary darkness and is gone until the next nightfall: only Rule 6 ends it. RULE 4, THE TAKEN: one it takes vanishes into the dark and is found in the room where it began, at the foot of the Number Two air shaft behind the 7 North seal, alive, cold, unconscious and unharmed, and is held there in the dark for nine days and nine nights; then they are gone. A living hand that reaches them before the ninth midnight can bring them out. RULE 5, ACCOUNTED FOR (the ward): a flame lit under a man's or woman's brass check on the lamp-house board, with their name said aloud, means that person is counted: the Dark cannot take them while that flame burns. A check stamped by hand by someone who knew the person counts as their own. Relighting the Kept Light under all fourteen checks, with all fourteen names said aloud, including Ezell Pettaway's, drives the Dark back below ground and holds it in 7 North: nobody is taken on the surface while the flame burns, but it is not laid, and if the flame goes out it comes up the same night. Thirteen names do nothing. RULE 6, LAID TO REST: by day it lies in the room where it began. It is laid to rest when that room is opened to the sun: direct sunlight falling into the barricade room at the foot of the Number Two air shaft, which means breaking the 1919 concrete cap off the shaft on Shumate's upper pasture and, on a clear day between eleven and one, throwing the sun down two hundred and twelve feet with a mirror held at the collar (the sun never stands straight overhead in West Virginia). Lamps, flares, magnesium and electric light do not count. Whatever is done on the surface, it knows. WHAT IT WANTS: what was done to Lafe Combs; someone alone, in the dark, for good. The fourteen are a separate thing: they are Shades (adversaries.json), they follow their own brass checks, and they knock.

campaignRules.name: Dread in Ottway
campaignRules.description: Use the Horror ruleset's fear checks and Dread (dread.json): a Wisdom saving throw against DC 10 for the sign of it, 15 for seeing it, 20 for the truth of it; failure gains 1 Dread, a natural 1 gains 2; the same horror costs Dread once per scene; knowing one of its rules lowers the DC by 2; darkness raises it by 2, and underground it is always dark outside the lamp. This campaign's horrors, by DC. 10: a lamp flame going small and blue in clean air; knocking under a floor, four and two; a brass check that is cold as creek ice in a warm room; frost on the grass around the air-shaft cap in April; the mules refusing the main heading; a grey man with a dark lamp at the drift mouth, gone when you look. 15: seeing the Dark, a darkness a lamp cannot reach, coming along a path toward you; the voice of someone taken calling your name from beside you; the fourteen Shades standing round the barricade; finding a taken person's light lying switched on and pointed at the drift mouth. 20: reading Lafe Combs's last note; the cap with its date stamped in the concrete; the truth that the company knew; seeing, in the barricade room, what the fourteen looked like at the end. Recovery is the ruleset's. In Ottway the once-a-day comfort can be a cup of coffee at Lettie's stove, a hymn at Mount Moriah or St. Stephen's, a pull from Garland's pint, a plate of ramps and fried potatoes at somebody's table, or a joke with the men waiting for the man-trip. Laying the Dark at the end drops everyone present to 0. The light goes out at the worst moment once per scenario, not more: a cap lamp's battery dying in the crawl, the coke ovens banked during the strike, the camp's power cut. Table safety: at the first session the GM asks what the players do not want in the game and honours any player's 'skip that' at once, without question, by cutting away. The 1919 deaths are on the page as knocking, notes, a cold room and names, never as bodies described; no child is taken, harmed or present at any dangerous scene; guards and miners are people with reasons, and nobody's people are the monster.

campaignRules.name: Rites That Work
campaignRules.description: Rites work only because a creature's rules say so, and anyone can perform them; an Occultist does them better (advantage, half the time). AGAINST THE DARK: NEVER ALONE (Rule 2): no roll; stay within arm's reach or answering voice, or tie a rope between you. The camp learns this rule faster than any other once someone says it aloud, and the union's habit of never sending a man to the company office alone becomes the camp's way of going home at night. ACCOUNTED FOR (Rule 5): hang the person's check, light a flame under it and say their name: Occult DC 10, one minute; anyone with their own company check can be protected this way, and any lamp will do if it stays lit. Imre has nine of the fourteen checks and Ezell's hand-stamped one; Superintendent Bledsoe has four in his desk; any check lost can be stamped again by someone who knew the man. THE KEPT LIGHT (Rule 5): the fourteen together, the lamp lit, all fourteen names said by people who knew them, Occult DC 13, ten minutes, in the lamp house or anywhere the board is hung; Imre must say József Kertész's, Morris must say his brother's. LIGHT (Rule 3): an electric cap lamp, a bonfire, a flare, Frankie's flash lamp or the coke ovens are walls; a flare fired into it does fire damage. THE OPENING (Rule 6): see the Blackdamp's Rules; breaking the cap is six hours with sledges and bars for six people (Heavy Work helps) or a Sapper's charge (DC 13 to place it right; test the gas under the cap first, see the Underground rule); holding the mirror steady in the wind for the minute it takes is a DC 12 Dexterity check, with help. FOR THE FOURTEEN (Shades): they cannot cross a line of salt; each follows whoever carries its own brass check; each is laid when it is buried in the ground and its name is spoken at the grave by someone who knew who it was. WRONG RITES do nothing, and the Dark knows you tried: holy water, a priest's blessing on the seal, a prayer for the dead said over the drift mouth, dynamite in 7 North (see firedamp), shooting into it, and burning the Kept Light's checks to 'send them on'.

campaignRules.name: Company and Union
campaignRules.description: Ottway is a town at war in slow motion, and the party will be counted by both sides. Track two scores for the party as a whole, from 0 to 5, in world state, and tell the players when either changes. COMPANY SUSPICION: rises for being seen at Mount Moriah on a Sunday night, asking about 7 North, photographing the tipple, visiting the jail, being out after the shift whistle, crossing Captain Kincaid, and for anything printed. 2: a guard follows you. 3: your mail is opened, the store will not serve you, and the doctor's or reporter's welcome is withdrawn. 4: Ironwood men search your room and you are told to be on Monday's train. 5: you are arrested on a county warrant, or put on the train with your bags thrown after you, or worse at the dead line at night. It falls when Bledsoe or the office is given a reason to think you useful. UNION TRUST: rises for keeping a secret, standing with a family being evicted, getting a man out of the Gale jail, carrying the Local's books, telling the truth about 1919 at a meeting, and for going down after Dewey. 2: the Local lets you into Sunday meetings. 3: miners will hide you, drive you, lie for you. 4: the Local will act when you ask it to: a crowd at the office, a strike, a crew with tools. 5: they will follow you into 7 North. It falls for being seen in the company office, carrying a badge, and for anything that puts a man's name in the company's hands. A party can hold high scores on both only through Dr. Ketterly, Garland Hensley or Lonzo Cutright, and only for so long. Violence: the guards are armed and deputised and the law is theirs in Selden County; shooting a guard is murder in the eyes of the court in Gale, and the camp will pay for it. The union in 1927 does not win: history says the southern fields organise in 1933. What the camp can win in April 1927 is its dead, the truth, and its men out of jail.

campaignRules.name: Underground
campaignRules.description: Ottway No. 3 is a room-and-pillar drift mine: entries driven into the coal, rooms turned off them, pillars of coal left to hold the roof, a seam five feet high, so a tall man walks stooped. 7 North runs a mile and a quarter north under the ridge from the main heading. LIGHT: an electric cap lamp lasts 10 hours, lights 10 feet brightly and never warns you of gas; a carbide lamp burns 4 hours on a charge, an open flame; a flame safety lamp is dim but is the only instrument the camp has for gas. BLACKDAMP (dead air, short of oxygen): sits in old workings, dips and behind seals; a safety lamp's flame dwindles and dies in it before a man feels anything; in it, a Constitution save DC 12 each 10 minutes or one level of exhaustion, and a creature at three levels is unconscious. It puts out flames, and so does the Dark: the GM never tells the players which it is until they test. FIREDAMP (methane): gathers at the roof, under seals and under the shaft cap; a safety lamp shows a blue cap over the flame (Mechanics DC 10 to read it); an open flame, a spark or a charge in it explodes (8d6 fire, DEX save DC 15 for half, and the roof comes down); a seal or the cap must be vented before it is broken. ROOF: a sounding rod tells drummy roof from sound (Mechanics or Perception DC 12); a fall is 4d6 bludgeoning and a trapped person needs Heavy Work or four people. THE SEALS: two masonry stoppings of concrete block across 7 North's two entries, three feet thick; four hours to break through with bars and sledges, an hour with a charge (and see firedamp). THE SHUMATE HOLE-THROUGH: from Mavis's grandfather's country bank on the far side of the ridge, a crawlway of four hundred yards, two feet high in places, with a flooded dip, into old rooms at the north end of 7 North, bricked up by the company in 1916 and never on the seal plan; nobody but Mavis and Lonzo knows it is there. THE BARRICADE ROOM: a cross-cut at the foot of the Number Two air shaft, walled off by the fourteen in 1919 with brattice cloth and gob. Time underground is lamp hours; count them.

explorationRules: Ottway is a single hollow and the map is a schematic of it: the depot and store at the bottom left, the rows climbing both sides of Kettle Run, the drift mouth, tipple and lamp house at the head of the hollow, the boss row on the dry hill, the Hill and Mount Moriah across the creek, Shumate Ridge and its farm above everything, 7 North under the ridge's northern shoulder, and Gale off the edge of the map fourteen miles down the valley. From the depot to the drift mouth is a twenty-minute walk; from the drift mouth up the ridge road to the Shumate farm is an hour, or forty minutes straight up through the laurel with Mavis; from the drift mouth to the 7 North seals is forty minutes by man-trip and an hour and a half on foot; from the Shumate country bank through the hole-through to the barricade room is three hours of crawling. Gale is forty minutes in Della's Ford, an hour by the morning or evening train, and four hours on foot; the Ironwood car at the dead line stops everyone after dark. The company's electric plant lights the boss row, the office, the store and the drift mouth; the rows have kerosene and whatever the coke ovens give, and when the company banks the ovens or cuts the plant the whole camp goes dark. The unit of play is the day and the night: tell the players the date and the weather every morning, and keep the nine-day count where they can see it.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a creature's rules, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Ottway, Kettle Run, Shumate Ridge, Selden County, Gale, the Ottway Smokeless Coal Company, Ottway No. 3, the 7 North explosion of 1919, the Ironwood Detective Agency, the Allegheny Labor Herald, Local 5512 and every person in the campaign are fictional, and the fourteen dead are invented men; no real disaster or its victims are used. The southern West Virginia coalfields, company towns, scrip, the company store, mine guards from detective agencies, yellow-dog contracts, evictions, the mine wars of 1912 to 1921, the 1927 strike in the northern fields, the United Mine Workers of America, racial segregation of camps, churches and schools, room-and-pillar drift mining, sealing mine fires, blackdamp and firedamp are real; no real person appears.
controlFile.theTruth: At 10:40 on the morning of Tuesday 14 October 1919, a pocket of firedamp at the 7 North face, set off by an open carbide flame, exploded and set the coal afire. Nineteen men working outby got out, some burned; fourteen men working inby, at the face and in the last rooms, were cut off by fire and afterdamp: Lafe Combs, 52; Vito Palermo, 30; József Kertész, 38; Wiktor 'Vic' Wojcik, 27; Moses Hairston, 41; Ezell Pettaway, 26; Marion Odum, 45, and his son Coy Odum, 19; Arvel Keene, 33; Gentry Absher, 36; Giuseppe 'Joe' Arcuri, 29; Pál Szűcs, 50; Ennis Mullins, 23; and Delbert Ratliff, 31. Lafe Combs, the oldest, led them away from the fire to the one place he knew had air: the foot of the Number Two air shaft, sunk in 1909 and abandoned under a rotten timber cap in 1916, where air still seeped down and, at noon, a grey thread of daylight came through the cracks. They walled off the cross-cut there with brattice cloth and gob and settled to wait, as they had been taught. On Wednesday 15 October, mine foreman Elwood Bledsoe, with the District Mine Inspector Orval Overbey's concurrence, had two masonry stoppings built across 7 North's entries to smother the fire: accepted practice, and the inspector believed what Bledsoe told him, that no one inby could be alive. On Thursday 16 October the seal crew, seven men under Lonzo Cutright, among them Washington Burchett and Hobart Lilly, heard knocking on the track rail: four and two, the old signal for men alive. Bledsoe came down and listened and said it was squeeze, the mountain settling over a fire, and that unless the seals were finished the fire would take the mine; the crew finished them. Bledsoe telegraphed Philadelphia. The answer came from the company president, J. Rinehart Ottway, on Friday morning: PROTECT PROPERTY. FIRE MUST BE STARVED. NO MEN TO ENTER. Bledsoe sent a truck, a mixer, two carpenters and two company guards up the ridge road and capped the Number Two air shaft with two feet of concrete, stamped O.S.C.Co. 10-17-19 in the wet surface, to cut off the air feeding the fire. Cletus Shumate, who had heard the knocking through the old timbers, was walked back to his house at gunpoint. The fire did go out, in three days. The men behind the seal lived six more days in the dark, on their lamps' last carbide and then on nothing, writing on the timbers in chalk, and the seal crew and the fire bosses heard them knocking, fainter, until Thursday 23 October. Something came into that room on the day the light was capped out of it, and it has no name and needs none: it took the ones who went alone in the dark, for water, for a look at the seal, one by one, and the last to die was Lafe Combs, alone, after the others, with his lamp out. The company listed thirteen dead, killed instantly by the explosion; Ezell Pettaway, who loaded on Moses Hairston's check No. 230, was not on its books and the office told his brother there was no such man. The inquest heard no word of knocking; Washington Burchett, asked, did not answer and was excused. Each of the seven seal-crew men was credited fifty dollars in scrip, 'special work, 7 North', on 18 October. Bledsoe became superintendent in 1921. The company has carried 7 North on its books as a sealed fire area ever since, to keep the inspectors out of it. Imre Halász kept his light. On 1 March 1927 it was put out; on the night of 25 March the Dark took Lester Gaither off the tipple; on 10 April it takes Dewey Spradlin; and the company has decided, under pressure from Philadelphia, to reopen 7 North for its coal on 2 May with new men, which means that whoever goes in first will find the notes on the timbers. Bledsoe means that to be him. Captain Arliss Kincaid of the Ironwood agency has his own orders from Philadelphia: break the Local first, and let nobody into 7 North before the company's own crew.
suspects: Superintendent Elwood Bledsoe, 56, a mining engineer from Pennsylvania who came up from the face: a careful, intelligent, decent-mannered man who has lived eight years with what he did on 17 October 1919 and has become, to survive it, exactly what the company needs. He did not want the men to die; he believed for one day that they were dead, and then he chose the mine. He keeps four of the fourteen brass checks in the bottom drawer of his desk, and the Philadelphia telegram under them. He wants 7 North reopened quietly, by himself first, so he can wash the timbers. He can be turned, once, by someone who shows him a way out that is not a lie; a man is alive behind his seal again, and he knows it.

Captain Arliss Kincaid, 44, commanding the Ironwood Detective Agency's twenty-two guards at Ottway: a former Army provost sergeant, efficient, unhurried, without malice and without pity, who believes that order is the only kindness a coal camp can afford. He put out the Kept Light on 1 March because his orders said no open flame in the lamp house, and he would do it again. He wants the Local broken before the strike reaches the southern field and the company's crew into 7 North on schedule. He is no villain to himself and should not be played as one; he is the most dangerous man in the campaign because he is always reasonable.

Vinton Plumley, 50, the store manager, who keeps the ledgers and knows what every family owes to the penny: he wrote the seven $50 'special work' credits in October 1919 in his own hand, and he is the company's eyes in the camp. He is frightened of Kincaid, contemptuous of the miners, and very fond of his own daughter, who teaches at the white school; he can be bought, and he can be frightened, and he will sell anyone.

Sheriff Boyd Sizemore of Selden County, 60, whose deputies' salaries the coal operators pay: he jailed Angelo Marchetti and Hobart Lilly for the murder of a man whose body was never found, because Kincaid asked him to. He is not cruel, only owned. A body would let him off the hook, and he would be grateful.

Hobart Lilly, 47, in the Gale jail: a loader, a Local man and one of the seal crew in 1919. He joined the union because of what he did. He did not kill Lester Gaither and he knows exactly what took him, because he has been hearing the knocking in his sleep for eight years.

J. Rinehart Ottway, the company president in Philadelphia, who never appears: the man who sent the telegram. Nothing in the campaign can touch him except a story printed where his board of directors will read it.
redHerrings: The union killed Lester Gaither. Captain Kincaid and the sheriff say so: Angelo Marchetti and Hobart Lilly argued with Gaither at the store over a short weight on Lilly's car, and Gaither vanished that night. They were at home in bed, and Garland Hensley knows Gaither was alone on the tipple. Gaither's body, at the barricade, with his Ironwood badge and his own chalk mark on a timber, clears them.

The guards took Dewey Spradlin. The Local thinks so: Dewey was a Local man, he vanished on the night of a meeting, and the Ironwood car was seen on the county road. It was not them; Kincaid wants to know what happened to Dewey nearly as badly as Della does, because two of his own men have quit since.

It is gas, or squeeze, or a pump. Bledsoe says the knocking is squeeze, and Lonzo's instruments show blackdamp behind the seal, which does put lamps out. The air behind the seal is bad, but squeeze does not knock four and two, and blackdamp does not walk up a creek path.

It is the fourteen come back for revenge. The grey men at the drift mouth are the fourteen, but they are not hunting anyone: they follow their checks, they knock, and they want to be brought out and buried. The Dark is something else, and it is the thing that takes.

It is something the immigrants or the Black miners brought, or something in the mountain from before. Some people in the camp will say both. Neither is true and the GM never lets it be: the Dark began on 23 October 1919, in the room where a man was left to die alone, and nobody's people or faith had anything to do with it.
clues: A. A MAN IS ALIVE BEHIND THE SEAL, AND HAS NINE DAYS (RULE 4). A1: the knocking on the 7 North track rail at the seal, 3:10 a.m. Monday 11 April, heard by Lonzo Cutright and by anyone with him; four and two, then answering when answered (bd-scenario-001). A2: the knocking under Lettie Burchett's kitchen floor since 1 March, which on Monday morning begins to answer back (bd-scenario-001). A3: Lonzo's fire-boss book: 'knocking, 7N seal' every morning from 28 March to 3 April, then nothing: nine days for Lester Gaither (bd-scenario-001 or 002). A4: 1919's nine days: the explosion on the 14th in the inquest transcript, the knocking until the 23rd in Bledsoe's words to Imre ('It's quit, Imre'), and the date on Mount Moriah's memorial page, 23 October (bd-scenario-002). A5: Morris Pettaway hears the rail on night shift (bd-scenario-001).

B. IT TAKES ONLY THE ALONE (RULE 2). B1: both disappearances side by side: Gaither alone on the tipple for ten minutes, his flashlight left on and pointing at the drift mouth; Dewey alone on the creek path after leaving the meeting early, his carbide lamp found cold on the path (bd-scenario-001). B2: Garland Hensley's account of 25 March (bd-scenario-001). B3: Vesta Spradlin and her neighbour Dovie Hensley saw something dark come down the creek path at eleven on 10 April while they stood together in Vesta's doorway with a lamp, and it went past them and on (bd-scenario-001 or 002). B4: Imre's old saying, from Old Lore or asked: never let a man go down alone, the dark is hungry (bd-scenario-002). B5: Lafe Combs's notes: when Coy Odum went for water alone it took him, and it does not come while they are all together (bd-scenario-003).

C. THE KEPT LIGHT CALLED IT AND CAN HOLD IT (RULES 1 AND 5). C1: Imre Halász's account of the lamp, 15 October 1919 to 1 March 1927 (bd-scenario-002). C2: Captain Kincaid's order book in the guards' shanty: '1 Mar. Lamp house cleared for new equipment. Open flame extinguished. Old checks discarded.' and the dark rectangle on the lamp-house wall (bd-scenario-001 or 002). C3: Lonzo's fire-boss book from 2 March: lamps going blue in the 7 North entries with no gas on the instrument, the mules refusing the main heading (bd-scenario-002). C4: Rev. Greer remembers Imre telling him, years ago, that he kept 'a light for the ones not counted up' (bd-scenario-002). C5: the dates: nobody taken in seven and a half years while the light burned, the first three weeks after it went out (any). C6: Lettie's Thin Place in the lamp house: a small steady flame, names said one after another, and the feeling of being counted (bd-scenario-002).

D. THE FOURTEENTH NAME (EZELL PETTAWAY). D1: Morris Pettaway (bd-scenario-001). D2: the company's tonnage sheets for September and October 1919 in the office or the store ledger room: check No. 230, Moses Hairston, loading twice the coal of any other man, two men's work on one number (bd-scenario-002). D3: Imre's hand-stamped check, E P, no number (bd-scenario-002). D4: Mount Moriah's register, the memorial page of fourteen names (bd-scenario-002). D5: Lafe Combs's list on the barricade timber, fourteen names, Ezell's among them (bd-scenario-003).

E. THE COMPANY KNEW THEY WERE ALIVE AND CAPPED THEIR AIR (THE TRUTH). E1: the cap on Shumate's pasture, stamped O.S.C.Co. 10-17-19, three days after the explosion, two after the seal (bd-scenario-001 or 002). E2: the store ledger, 18 October 1919, seven credits of $50 'special work, 7N', and Lettie's unspent slip (bd-scenario-002). E3: the inquest transcript's unanswered question (Dr. Ketterly), and the District Inspector's own field notebook in the Gale courthouse inquest file, which records 'signals reported at seal 16th and 17th, Supt. advises squeeze' (bd-scenario-002). E4: Wash Burchett's deathbed words to Lettie (bd-scenario-001). E5: Lonzo Cutright's confession (bd-scenario-002). E6: the fourteen's chalk notes, dated 16 to 23 October 1919 (bd-scenario-003). E7: the Philadelphia telegram under the checks in Bledsoe's drawer (bd-scenario-002 or 004).

F. HOW IT ENDS: THE ROOM WHERE IT BEGAN, OPENED TO THE SUN (RULE 6). F1: Lafe Combs's notes: the grey light through the shaft cracks at dinner time keeps it off them, and then the light and the air stop (bd-scenario-003). F2: Mavis's frost ring round the cap, the Corpse Light walking over it at night (it burns over Lester Gaither, unburied below), and at first light the darkness draining back down to the cap like water to a drain (bd-scenario-002 or 003). F3: Lettie's Listener in the barricade room: Lafe Combs's last words, 'Somebody open it. Let some light in here.' (bd-scenario-003). F4: Old Lore, Hunter of the Uncanny or Imre's Collector clue: daylight is the one lamp it cannot put out (any). F5: Lonzo's 1919 map and his arithmetic: the shaft is two hundred and twelve feet straight down onto the barricade room, and the sun never stands overhead here, so it will need a glass (bd-scenario-003 or 004).
controlFile.theKeyClue: The players solve Ottway when they stop asking what the Dark is and start asking who was left alone, and by whom. Everything turns on the nine days: the nine days Lester Gaither knocked, the nine days the fourteen knocked, and the nine days Dewey Spradlin has. Point bd-scenario-001 hard at A and B, so the party know on Monday that a man is alive and why he was taken; let bd-scenario-002 give them C, D and E, the whole crime and the Kept Light, while the town divides; let bd-scenario-003 put them in the barricade room with the notes, and Dewey, and the one clue to F they could not have found anywhere else; and let bd-scenario-004 be about whether the town will stand together long enough, on a ridge in the noon sun, to finish it.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. THE DARK: it is laid only by Rule 6. If the cap is broken and the sun thrown down on a clear noon, the barricade room fills with plain daylight for the first time, there is a sound from the shaft like a long breath let out, every lamp in Ottway No. 3 burns yellow and steady, and everyone present drops to 0 Dread; that night nobody in the camp keeps a lamp lit out of fear, and nothing comes. If the Kept Light is relit and never laid, the Dark is held in 7 North for as long as someone keeps the flame, and the company's crew on 2 May walks into it. If nothing is done, 2 May is the second 7 North disaster. DEWEY SPRADLIN: brought out before midnight on 19 April, he lives, and remembers nothing but cold and voices; after it, he is the fifteenth name. THE FOURTEEN: brought up into daylight and buried, each under his own name, Ezell Pettaway's spoken by his brother and carried home to Hale County, they are laid, and the knocking stops for good. THE TRUTH: Lafe Combs's notes, the cap, the ledger and the telegram, photographed and printed in the Allegheny Labor Herald and picked up by the wire, cost J. Rinehart Ottway his presidency within the year and the company its lease on No. 3 within two; a grand jury in Gale will not indict Bledsoe, because this is Selden County in 1927, but the state will reopen the inquest, and the camp will hear its dead named out loud. If the notes are lost, burned by Bledsoe or taken by Kincaid, the company's story stands. THE JAIL: Lester Gaither's body clears Angelo Marchetti and Hobart Lilly. THE STRIKE: Local 5512 comes out or does not, and loses either way in 1927; but if the camp stood together on the last night and on the ridge, it does not break, and six years later it is the first local in Selden County to sign a contract. BLEDSOE: if he is given the chance and takes it, he goes into 7 North with the party, or swings a sledge on the cap, or hands over the telegram, and is ruined, and is a little less alone. KINCAID: he leaves on the train with his men when the company stops paying, and he is the last person to put his light out.
